setupSteps: Self-powered vs plugged in. Many commercial bikes are self-powered: the screen wakes only when you start pedalling. Pedal for a few seconds.
Quick Start / Manual. The simplest choice: a timer starts at the lowest level, and you change the level with ▲/▼ or + / −.

Resistance levels. Usually 1 to 16, 20, 25 or 30 depending on the brand (e.g. some Life Fitness recumbents list 20 levels, some Platinum models 26). Level numbers are NOT comparable across brands. Pick by effort.
RPM. Pedal revolutions per minute (one full circle of one pedal). Some bikes show "speed" in km/h; on a bike this is a calculated figure, not real road speed.

Watts. Many consoles show your power output in watts. This is the most useful number on the screen, because the Compendium MET values for stationary cycling are listed by watts (see section 10). If your console shows watts, use it to estimate calories.

Constant-power vs constant-resistance mode. Some bikes (often in heart-rate or "constant watts" programs) hold your watts steady: if you pedal faster, the resistance drops, and if you pedal slower it gets heavier. In normal Manual mode, resistance stays at the level you chose.

Programs. Common names: Manual, Hill/Rolling Hills, Interval, Random, Fat Burn, Cardio, Heart-Rate Control (HRC/Target HR), Constant Watts, Fitness Test. Beginners should start on Manual to stay in control.
Weight and age entry. Enter your real weight and age if asked; the machine uses them for calories and heart-rate targets.

Heart-rate grips. Metal pads on the handlebars (upright) or side handles (recumbent). Hold both still and lightly for a reading. Use RPE and the talk test as your main guide; a chest strap is more accurate if the console accepts one.

Calories display. A rough guide only. Press coverage of UCSF testing reported that cardio machines overestimate calories by about 19% on average, with the stationary bike the least wrong at about 7% (secondary source; original study not found).

Stop / Pause. Simply stop pedalling. Most bikes pause and then reset after a while. Gym exercise bikes have no safety key or clip, because the pedals only move when you drive them. Exception: spin bikes / indoor cycles often have a fixed-gear flywheel that keeps the pedals turning; stop them by slowing your legs gradually or pressing the red brake/resistance knob down. Never try to step off while the pedals are still spinning.
Wipe the seat, handlebars and console with the gym spray or wipes.
Wear closed training shoes, laces tucked in. No loose dupatta, saree pallu, long scarf or hanging towel near the pedals or flywheel.

Stand beside the bike. Set the seat roughly level with the top of your hip bone (the iliac crest, the rounded bony ridge at your waist) (HSS method). Pull the pop-pin, slide the seat, release, then wiggle the seat until the pin clicks fully in.
Hold the handlebars, step over the frame and sit on the widest part of the saddle (your "sit bones" on the saddle, not the narrow nose).
Put the balls of your feet over the centre of each pedal. Tighten the straps so they are snug, not cutting in.

Check seat height. Pedal slowly and stop with one pedal at the very bottom (6 o'clock). Your knee should be slightly bent, roughly 25–35° short of straight (ACE Group Fitness guidance; Holmes method). A quick check: put your heel on the bottom pedal; your leg should be almost straight. When you put the ball of the foot back on, the soft bend appears. Your hips should not rock side to side when you pedal. Too high: hips rock, toes point down hard at the bottom, or you reach for the pedal. Lower one notch. Too low: knee comes up high and close to the chest at the top and stays well bent at the bottom; may cause front-of-knee ache. Raise one notch.

Check fore–aft (if adjustable). With the pedals level (3 and 9 o'clock), your front knee should sit roughly above the ball of the foot / pedal spindle (est.). If you see a lot of foot in front of the knee, slide the seat forward; if you see only toes, slide it back.
Handlebars (if adjustable). Level with the seat or slightly higher for beginners, so you do not hunch forward. Elbows soft, not locked.
Start pedalling slowly to wake the console. Choose Quick Start or Manual, set a low level (for example 2–4 on a 20-level bike; est.), enter age and weight if asked.
Wipe the seat, handles and console.
Step through the low frame (or over it) and sit back fully into the seat, low back against the backrest.
Pull the seat lever and slide the seat forward or back. Place the arch or heel of one foot on the pedal at its farthest point: the leg should be almost straight. Lock the lever, check it is secure.

Now put the balls of your feet on the pedals and tighten the straps. At the farthest point, your knee should have a soft bend, roughly the same 25–35° short of straight as on the upright (est.; no specific standard found for recumbents).
At the closest point, your knee should not come up near your chest or press uncomfortably. If it does, slide the seat back one notch.
If the backrest reclines, start at a more upright setting (easier to see the console and less hip bend; est.).
Hold the side handles lightly. Start pedalling, choose Manual, low level.
Set seat height the same way, and set the saddle fore–aft and handlebar height as above.
Learn where the resistance knob and emergency brake are before you start (pressing down on the knob usually stops the flywheel).
Keep some resistance on; spinning with no resistance on a fixed flywheel lets the pedals run away from you.

steps.title: Start pedalling forward slowly
steps.tempo: about 60–70 RPM for the first minute (est.).
steps.visualCheck: side – hips still on the seat, upper body quiet. Front – knees moving straight up and down over the feet.

steps.title: Sit on your sit bones (upright) or sit back fully (recumbent)
steps.feel: weight on the two bony points under your buttocks, not on the soft tissue in front; on the recumbent, low back supported by the backrest.
steps.visualCheck: side – upright rider has a tall spine with a slight forward lean from the hips; recumbent rider's back stays in contact with the backrest.

steps.title: Hold the handlebars or side handles lightly
steps.feel: hands resting, not gripping; shoulders relaxed and down.
steps.visualCheck: front – shoulders level, elbows soft, wrists straight.

steps.title: Push through the ball of the foot from the top of the stroke
steps.feel: front of the thigh and buttock working as the pedal moves from about 12 o'clock to 5 o'clock (upright) or from the closest to the farthest point (recumbent).
steps.visualCheck: side – foot roughly flat to slightly toe-down; heel does not drop sharply.

steps.title: Let the pedal come back up without stomping
steps.feel: the leg follows the pedal round; the back of the thigh and front of the hip lightly help lift (more if you use straps).
steps.visualCheck: the knee comes up smoothly; no bouncing on the saddle.

steps.title: Keep the knees in line
steps.feel: knees track over your second toe throughout.
steps.visualCheck: front – knees neither fall in towards the frame nor flare out.

steps.title: Warm up: 5 minutes, easy effort
steps.feel: breathing rises slightly; you can chat easily.

steps.title: Raise resistance 1–2 levels at a time to your working effort
steps.breathing: you can talk but not sing (moderate).
steps.tempo: wait 30–60 seconds after each change before judging (est.).
steps.visualCheck: if you start rocking, bouncing, or pedalling below about 60 RPM, the resistance is too heavy for now (avoid heavy resistance that forces you below about 60 RPM; this strains the knees).

steps.title: Hold your working pace for the planned time (section 7)
steps.feel: steady effort you could keep up for the planned minutes.
steps.tempo: about 70–90 RPM for steady riding (est.; beginners may be comfortable nearer 60–70).

steps.title: (Upright only, optional, later) Stand up out of the saddle for short climbs
Cool down: 3–5 minutes at low resistance
Slow down and stop
steps.visualCheck: pedals fully stopped (on a spin bike, use the brake).

steps.title: Get off safely
steps.feel: steady. If dizzy or light-headed, sit back down or hold the frame for a moment.

steps.title: Wipe the seat, handles and console

commonMistakes.title: Seat too low
commonMistakes.text: Seat too low. Very common in shared gym bikes left at someone else's setting. More knee bend all the way round; a 2022 review found patellofemoral (kneecap) compressive force seems to rise as saddle height drops (evidence is small and mixed). Fix: raise the seat until there is a soft 25–35° bend at the bottom.

commonMistakes.title: Seat too high
commonMistakes.text: Seat too high. Hips rock, toes point hard, and the back of the knee overstretches; can irritate the hamstrings and back of the knee. Fix: lower until hips stay still.

commonMistakes.title: Recumbent seat too far or too close
commonMistakes.text: Recumbent seat too far or too close. Too far = reaching and locked knees; too close = knees jammed up near the chest. Fix: re-do the "nearly straight with the heel" check.

commonMistakes.title: Grinding heavy resistance at very low RPM
commonMistakes.text: Grinding heavy resistance at very low RPM. Pushing big resistance below about 60 RPM loads the knees heavily. Fix: lower resistance and keep 60–90 RPM.

commonMistakes.title: No resistance, flailing fast
commonMistakes.text: No resistance, flailing fast. The flywheel does the work, you bounce on the seat and the training effect is small. Fix: add resistance until each push has a little weight behind it.

commonMistakes.title: Hunching over the bars or slouching on the recumbent
commonMistakes.text: Hunching over the bars or slouching on the recumbent. Sustained low-back flexion is linked to discomfort in cyclists; lower handlebars mean more lumbar flexion. Fix: raise the bars if you can, hinge from the hips, or use the recumbent's backrest.

commonMistakes.title: Sitting on the saddle nose / ignoring numbness
commonMistakes.text: Sitting on the saddle nose / ignoring numbness. Pressure on the soft tissue between the sit bones can cause genital numbness or tingling. Fix: sit back on the wide part, wear padded shorts if available, stand up or shift position every 10–15 minutes on long rides, and choose the recumbent's wide seat. Numbness that lasts after the ride needs a doctor.

commonMistakes.title: Watching the phone in your lap
commonMistakes.text: Watching the phone in your lap. Rounds the upper back and neck. Fix: phone on the console shelf at eye level, or listen instead.

commonMistakes.title: Trusting the calorie number
commonMistakes.text: Trusting the calorie number. Fix: use the MET estimates in section 10, ideally from the watts reading.

commonMistakes.title: Getting off a spin bike while the flywheel is still spinning
commonMistakes.text: Getting off a spin bike while the flywheel is still spinning. Fix: slow down, press the brake, wait for a full stop.

safetyNotes: Knee problems: usually one of the best cardio choices. Set the seat height carefully (too low raises front-of-knee load), avoid heavy resistance below 60 RPM, and stop if pain rises during or after riding. One orthopaedic surgeon quoted in consumer press allows cycling for mild-to-moderate arthritis but not for severe arthritis or certain knee injuries, so ask your doctor if your knee is badly affected.
Low-back problems: the recumbent supports the back; on the upright, raise the bars and avoid hunching. Lower bars and sustained lumbar flexion are linked to low-back discomfort in cyclists.
Shoulder, wrist or hand problems: rest the hands lightly; the recumbent needs almost no upper-body support.
High blood pressure or heart disease: moderate effort, longer warm-up and cool-down, never hold your breath, no all-out sprints unless your doctor agrees.

Pregnancy: ACOG lists stationary cycling as safe in uncomplicated pregnancy and advises avoiding activities with a high fall risk; a stationary bike removes the fall risk of outdoor cycling. As the bump grows, raise the handlebars or use the recumbent, stay at a talk-test effort and avoid overheating.

Numbness or tingling in the groin, or in the feet (e.g. diabetic nerve damage): sit on the sit bones, use a wide seat (recumbent), take short standing breaks, check your feet after riding. Persistent numbness needs a doctor.

Recent surgery: only with clearance from your surgeon or physiotherapist. After knee replacement, bikes are commonly used in rehab, often starting with a raised seat and no resistance; riding full circles comfortably on an upright usually needs about 100° of knee bend, and a recumbent may need less.

Stop immediately if: chest pain or pressure; unusual breathlessness; dizziness or feeling faint; irregular or racing heartbeat; sharp joint pain; numbness that does not settle. Seek medical help for chest symptoms.
Hazards: keep children, hands, towels and loose clothing away from pedals and flywheel; spin-bike flywheels can keep spinning; check the seat pin is fully locked before sitting.

Gym etiquette: wipe the seat and handles (sweat collects on the saddle); many Indian gyms set a 20–30-minute limit at peak hours (est.), so check the notice board; do not "reserve" a bike with a towel; reset the seat lever and console when done is optional, but leave the area clear.
